title: Heavier than the earth
hookLine: Yudhishthira reads the shore, agrees to answer, and calls a mother heavier than the earth
carry: honor parents: heavier than earth, higher than sky

cards: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it.
He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks.
Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.

teach.b: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. No wounds on his brothers. No footprints of an enemy.
Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes.

teach.h: I AM A CRANE. WHO ARE YOU?
teach.b: I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth.
No bird could do this, Yudhishthira says. Who are you? And he sees a yaksha, a huge spirit, speaking from up in a tree.
Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. I don't want what's yours, he says. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able.

teach.h: HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.
teach.b: What is heavier than the earth? A mother. What is higher than the sky?
A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind.
What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family.
This is one of Hinduism's oldest teachings.

teach.h: LET YOUR MOTHER BE A GOD TO YOU.
teach.b: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with these words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you.
It's why Hindu children bow and touch the feet of their parents and elders, and get a hand on the head and a blessing back. Not because elders are always right.
Because what they carried for you weighs more than the earth.

how: In the epic, the yaksha's questions often sound like riddles, and Yudhishthira's first answers here point to mother and father; Hindu children honor parents and elders by touching their feet.

o: a riddle contest held at a king's court
the yaksha's questions, asked at the lake
a vow of silence kept beside sacred water

games.q: the first answers — tap the pairs.

s: Yudhishthira found wounds on his brothers
there were no wounds and no footprints, which is why he suspected something more than an enemy.
the voice first claimed to be a crane
Yudhishthira said no bird could do this, and asked who it really was.
touching an elder's feet means they are always right
it honors what they carried for you: let your mother be a god to you, the Upanishad says.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. four brothers lie dead by the lake, you're dying of thirst, and a voice says answer first. what do you do?
o: drink quickly, before the voice can stop you.
ask who it is, and agree to answer.
games.why: he asks who it is, sees a yaksha, and says: I don't want what's yours. ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able.

practice: Bring to mind your mother, your father, or whoever raised you, or an elder who has been good to you. Let their face come clear, and remember one thing they carried for you.

If they're living, plan a pranam: touch their feet next time you see them, or call and ask their blessing. If they've died, or it's complicated, hold them as you can. If you pray, bring them into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions, which Yudhishthira is the first to answer. The brother who stops to look, offers to answer, and names a mother heavier than the earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions; prashna means a question.

carryVoice: Your line: honor parents, heavier than earth, higher than sky. A mother, a father, a mind, a field of thoughts. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: Yudhishthira at the lake; the crane and the yaksha; the first questions (heavier than the earth, higher than the sky, faster than the wind, more numerous than grass)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (the teacher's parting words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you)
Touching the feet of parents and elders (pranam, charan sparsh), in general
